overlap.title: Overlap ratio
overlap.description: Heavy overlap increases lexical recognition error by 27.2–38.6 percentage points and speaker-attribution error by 4.2–19.1 points across all seven systems.
overlap.control: Only inference units containing both classes are retained.
overlap.note: Heavy overlap (at least 50% of an utterance) is compared with no overlap within the same inference unit. Only units containing both conditions are retained.

metrics.definition: Change in lexical recognition error, in percentage points.
Change in speaker-attribution error, in percentage points.

similarity.title: Speaker similarity
similarity.description: Similar voices increase speaker confusion even without overlap. The association is significant for all seven systems (Spearman ρ = 0.248–0.323).
similarity.note: Analysis uses completely non-overlapping utterances. Directional confusion is the fraction of aligned tokens from one speaker attributed to the other.

metrics.definition: Spearman correlation between pairwise speaker similarity and directional speaker confusion.

acoustic.title: Acoustic quality
acoustic.description: Acoustic degradation primarily increases lexical recognition errors. It is also associated with shorter predicted speech timelines in six of seven systems; its association with attribution error is weak.
acoustic.control: Computed on non-overlapping utterances away from speaker switches. R_time measures duration contraction, not boundary displacement.
acoustic.note: Analysis uses non-overlapping utterances away from speaker switches. R_time = T_hyp / T_ref measures predicted-to-reference speech duration, rather than timestamp-boundary displacement.

metrics.definition: Correlation of acoustic degradation with lexical recognition error.
Correlation of acoustic degradation with speaker-attribution error.
Correlation of acoustic degradation with the predicted-to-reference speech duration ratio R_time.

turn.title: Speaker turn interval
turn.description: Near speaker switches, attribution error rises by 1.51–4.17 percentage points across all systems. Lexical recognition and segmentation errors show no significant change.
turn.control: E_lex and E_seg were not significant for any evaluated system.
turn.note: Within each inference unit, compare utterances near non-overlapping speaker switches (±0.5 seconds) with those far from all switches.

metrics.definition: Change in speaker-attribution error near speaker switches, in percentage points.

speaker.title: Speaker number
speaker.description: More speakers are associated with greater attribution difficulty after controlling for dataset and overlap. The association is positive in all six evaluated systems and significant in four.
speaker.control: P3 is excluded to reduce dataset-specific bias. Association does not imply causation; SoulX is not evaluated.
speaker.note: Center both variables by dataset and remove overlap effects. Exclude P3 (≥9 speakers) and SoulX-Transcriber’s 5-minute inputs. Association does not imply causation.

metrics.definition: Correlation of speaker number with speaker-attribution error after controlling for dataset and overlap.
